prayer.text: O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine, all praise and all thanksgiving be every moment thine.

cues.text: A Relic With a Long and Uncertain Road
Tradition traces the relic venerated at Weingarten Abbey, near Ravensburg in southern Germany, back to St. Longinus.
He was a Roman soldier remembered in Christian tradition, said to have caught earth mixed with drops of Christ's blood at the foot of the Cross.
From there, the account holds, the relic passed through the hands of emperors and counts across the centuries.
This included, tradition says, a rediscovery under Pope St. Leo IX in 1048, before finally coming into the possession of Judith of Flanders, wife of Welf I, Duke of Bavaria.
A Gift to the Abbey
According to the abbey's traditional account, Judith presented the relic to Weingarten's Benedictine monks on the Friday following the Feast of the Ascension.
The event was later commemorated annually as Blutfreitag , or "Blood Friday."
Devotional sources place this presentation anywhere from 1090 to 1094, a discrepancy that has never been fully resolved.
A History Modern Scholars Have Questioned
Historians studying the abbey's records have identified significant chronological and political difficulties in the traditional narrative as it has come down to us.
Some have concluded that key details were shaped or embellished in later centuries to lend the relic greater prestige and legitimacy.
This does not mean the relic's veneration at Weingarten is not genuinely ancient.
Record of the annual procession itself reaches back with certainty at least to the sixteenth century.
However, the specific circumstances of its arrival should be received as devotional tradition rather than settled documentary fact.
Legacy
Whatever uncertainty surrounds its precise origin, the devotion at Weingarten has endured in a form few Passion relics can match.

Each spring, thousands of riders carry the relic of the Precious Blood through the surrounding countryside in an annual procession still counted among Europe’s largest equestrian religious processions.
We recognize in this long, imperfectly documented tradition something true of much popular devotion across the centuries.
A community's faithfulness across nine hundred years of prayer can be real and enduring, even where historians continue to debate the precise paper trail behind its arrival.
